summary: A census ordered by Caesar Augustus brings Joseph and Mary from Nazareth to Bethlehem, where Jesus is born and laid in a manger.
key_insight: Luke never quotes Micah’s prophecy, but he shows it coming true. A decree from Rome, meant to count the emperor’s subjects, moved a couple from Nazareth to the one town where Israel’s Ruler was to be born (Micah 5:2).
story: In those days Caesar Augustus issued a decree that all the world should be registered. This census first took place while Quirinius was governing Syria, and everyone went to be registered in his own city. {Lk}

So Joseph went up from Nazareth in Galilee to Judea, to the city of David, which is called Bethlehem, because he was of the house and lineage of David. He went to be registered with Mary, his betrothed wife, who was with child. {Lk}
While they were there, the time came for Mary to give birth. {Lk} So Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judea, in the days of Herod the king. {Mt}
“She brought forth her firstborn Son, and wrapped Him in swaddling cloths, and laid Him in a manger, because there was no room for them in the inn.” {Lk}
differences: Matthew mentions the birth in a single clause, naming the town and the king, and moves straight on to the wise men.
Only Luke tells of the census, the journey from Nazareth, the swaddling cloths and the manger.
Matthew dates the birth by “Herod the king.” Luke dates it here by Caesar Augustus and Quirinius, governor of Syria, though he has already placed these events “in the days of Herod” (Luke 1:5).
Both name Bethlehem of Judea; Luke also calls it “the city of David.”

fit.question: Matthew places Jesus’ birth in the days of Herod, who died in 4 BC. Luke links it to a census taken while Quirinius governed Syria, and the best-known census under Quirinius came in AD 6. Can both be right?

points.label: A “first” census
points.text: Luke knew the later census well. In Acts he mentions the revolt of Judas of Galilee “in the days of the census” (Acts 5:37). By calling this one the “first,” he seems to set it apart from that famous one. Some also read Luke’s Greek as saying this registration came before the one Quirinius carried out as governor.

points.label: Quirinius’s earlier service
points.text: Quirinius served Rome in the East for many years before AD 6, including a military command in the region. Some think he held an earlier post connected with Syria, and that a registration begun under Herod became known by his name. Roman records for these years are incomplete.

fit.note: Outside records for these years are incomplete, and Luke, who dates events with care and knew of the later census, gives no sign of confusing the two.
fit.short: Luke knew the later census (Acts 5:37) and calls this one “first.” It may have preceded his, or Quirinius held an earlier role.

scene.label: Caesar Augustus
scene.text: Augustus ruled Rome from 31 BC to AD 14. He ended a century of civil wars, and his reign was celebrated as an age of peace. His decree, issued in Rome, reached a household in Nazareth.

scene.label: Bethlehem
scene.text: A small town in the hills just south of Jerusalem. Rachel was buried on the way to it (Genesis 35:19), Ruth gleaned in Boaz’s fields there, and David was born there and anointed king (1 Samuel 16:1–13). Its name means house of bread.

scene.label: “The inn”
scene.text: Luke’s word can mean an inn, but it often means a guest room; Luke uses it for the “guest room” of the Last Supper (Luke 22:11). Many think Joseph and Mary stayed in a crowded family home, where animals were brought into a lower area at night beside a feeding trough. Others picture a public lodging place. Either way, the Child was laid where animals ate.

scene.label: When
scene.text: Herod the Great died in 4 BC by most reckonings, so Jesus was born before that, probably between 6 and 4 BC. Our BC and AD system, worked out centuries later, missed by a few years. The Gospels give no month or day.

witnesses.matthew: Mentions the birth only in passing, in a clause that sets up the visit of the wise men. What matters to Matthew is the place, Bethlehem of Judea, which fulfills Micah’s prophecy (Matthew 2:5–6), and the king, Herod, whose rivalry with the true King drives the next chapter.
witnesses.luke: Sets the birth on the world stage, naming the emperor and the governor, and explains how a family from Nazareth came to be in Bethlehem. He tells it in a few plain sentences, and the details he keeps are humble ones: a long journey, swaddling cloths, a manger, no room.

seeing.reveals: The Son of the Highest entered the world as the child of a displaced couple, under a foreign emperor’s decree, and was laid in a feeding trough. He had no claim on any room, yet every power in the story, Caesar’s included, served God’s plan to bring Him to Bethlehem.
seeing.living: The census was an imposition and the journey was hard, yet God used both to keep a promise made through Micah some seven hundred years before. Decisions made far above you, by people who do not know your name, are not outside His rule. Trust Him in the places where you have no room and no say.
seeing.ponder: What disruption in your life have you only resented, when God may be using it to bring you where He wants you?

preaching.big_idea: Caesar issued the decree, but God was keeping His promise to bring the King to Bethlehem.
preaching.watch_for: In the Old Testament, “the City of David” usually means the stronghold of Zion in Jerusalem (2 Samuel 5:7). Luke twice uses the phrase for Bethlehem, David’s birthplace (2:4, 11). He points to the shepherd boy’s hometown, not the royal fortress.

title: Jesus Is Born in Bethlehem
